sources.title: Rosalía de Castro (Q464264), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): label 'Rosalía de Castro', English description 'Galician poet and writer (1837-1885)', born 23 February 1837, died July 1885 (Wikidata carries two day values, 15 and 22 July; the scholarly sources read give 15 July), instance of human, citizen of Spain; no Korean label and no Korean Wikipedia article. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Ingrid Martinez-Rico, 'Castro, Rosalia de (1837-1885)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale; reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls her one of the few women and few regional writers in the Spanish canon and a protagonist of the Galician cultural revival; says Cantares gallegos (1863), her first collection in Galician, was a crucial turning point for the literary status of a language relegated to oral tradition since the fifteenth century, that in its prologue she says she wants to defend her land and language from those who despise and mock them, that Follas novas (1880) gives Galician metaphysical and subjective themes it had been thought unfit for, and that En las orillas del Sar (1884, in Castilian) was praised for metrical experiment and admired by the Generation of 1898; also describes her novels, the satire El caballero de las botas azules, the article on women writers 'Las literatas', her Follas novas foreword preferring poems that voice the sorrows of those who suffer, and the loss of manuscripts she asked her family to destroy. Admiring reference entry that itself notes the 'little saint' mythologising; the entry's account of her illness and death is not used.

'Castro, Rosalia de', Gale Contextual Encyclopedia of World Literature (reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). Second Gale reference entry with a different author and series: calls her an acknowledged master of Spanish poetry who wrote mainly in Galician, credits Cantares gallegos as the catalyst of the nineteenth-century Galician revival, says her fluid, lilting metre contrasted with the rigid structures of her contemporaries and influenced later poets, and records a feminist reading of the first collection; it says her husband's prompting led her to publish the Galician songs (the other Gale entry says she was at first reluctant), and it ascribes her melancholy to her birth and later illness, claims that are not used here. Reference summary.

Marina Mayoral, 'Biografia de Rosalia de Castro' (in Galician), Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes portal on the author (read in full). Biography by a leading editor of her poetry: birth records and the childhood documents found in archives; her classes and successful acting at the Liceo de la Mocidade; her marriage in 1858 and seven children; Murguia's destruction of her letters to him and his shaping of her image; her 1864 letter to Eduardo Pondal saying none of her work satisfied her and that she had torn up what she wrote, the similar remark in the 1865 article 'Las literatas', her request to her daughters before she died to burn her manuscripts, and Mayoral's remark that she judged her own work modestly while being aware of her role in giving Galician back its status as a language of culture; anecdotes of her generosity retold by early biographers, which Mayoral warns belong to a mythified image. Mayoral's psychological and death-related interpretation of her poetry is the author's reading and is not used.

Victoria Alvarez Ruiz de Ojeda, 'Avances na investigacion da biografia rosaliana', Madrygal 21 (2018) 381-388 (journal article from a 2013 lecture, read in Galician from the repository PDF). Archive-based researcher's account: no documentary biography of Rosalia exists; Murguia, who outlived her, destroyed her correspondence, guarded her image and held that a woman should live 'without deeds and without biography'; she documents Rosalia's acting through a volume of twelve comedies staged at the Liceo de la Juventud in Santiago with her name written in by the stage director, notes that Santiago society then did not accept a girl performing in public, and describes her education as largely self-taught, the only evidence of her training being her own prologue to Cantares gallegos. Scholarly article.

Carlos Castelao, 'Maria Cardarelly, un lostrego na fotografia galega' (in Galician), study published by the Fundacion Rosalia de Castro (2017, read in part; the sections on Cardarelly's portraits of Rosalia). Used for the portrait only: says Cardarelly's studio carte-de-visite of Rosalia in the Real Academia Galega archive carries the stamp 'Fotografia de M.a Cardarelly, Santiago', that a second albumen print of the same sitting was found in 2013, that both were most plausibly taken around 1865 and not later than 1866 when Cardarelly stopped working in Santiago, and that the Fundacion Rosalia de Castro archive holds the second one. Not used for any scoring row.

Anxo Angueira, 'Unha primeira edicion de Cantares gallegos con fotografia, autografo e carta de Rosalia' (in Galician), Fundacion Rosalia de Castro (2013; read in part). Used for the portrait only: describes the 55 x 90 mm albumen carte-de-visite of Rosalia pasted into a bound first edition of Cantares gallegos (1863), beside a pencil note '15-VII-85' and a page with sixteen verses signed 'Rosalia Castro de Murguia', identifies it as a sibling of the Cardarelly print in the Real Academia Galega, and reproduces the page. Not used for any scoring row.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_rosalia_wiw, src_rosalia_galelit, src_rosalia_mayoral, src_rosalia_alvarez | 1857-1880 | reference entry, reference entry, biography, archival journal article] The Women in World History entry says her Cantares gallegos prologue sets out to defend the Galician language against those who mock it and that she later used Galician for metaphysical and subjective themes it had been thought unfit for; Mayoral credits her with giving Galician back its standing as a language of culture, and Alvarez shows she acted in public at the Liceo when Santiago society disapproved of girls performing. Counter-weight: the Galician movement was led by Murguia and she named Antonio Trueba's songs as a model, so the stance was shared, not hers alone. CONCENTRATION (agent): the two Gale entries are one reference family and the other two sources describe separate facets; lowered from 62 / 0.50 (strong_inference) to 58 / 0.44 (inference).

creative_originality.rationale: [src_rosalia_wiw, src_rosalia_galelit | 1863-1884 | reference entry, reference entry] The Women in World History entry says Cantares gallegos set a popular refrain before each poem and elaborated it, that Follas novas broke ground by using Galician for subjective themes, and that En las orillas del Sar was praised for metrical experiments anticipating later modernists; the Gale literature entry says her fluid metre set her apart from contemporaries bound to rigid forms. Both rest on the same critical tradition and neither names a specific creative process of hers. CONCENTRATION (agent): one reference family and no archival evidence; lowered from 66 / 0.50 (strong_inference) to 60 / 0.44 (inference).

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_rosalia_wiw, src_rosalia_mayoral | 1858-1884 | reference entry, biography] The Women in World History entry quotes her Follas novas foreword preferring poems that voice the sorrows of those who suffer around her, notes poems on emigration ('widows of the living') and on deforestation, and her 1858 text defending women; Mayoral retells accounts of her giving to the poor by early biographers but warns they belong to a mythified image. The evidence is her own stated aim and her subjects, not documented actions to change anything. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.44 to 54 / 0.38 because the claim rests on her own foreword and hagiographic anecdotes.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_rosalia_mayoral, src_rosalia_wiw | 1864-1885 | biography, reference entry] Mayoral quotes her 1864 letter to Pondal saying none of her work satisfied her and that she had torn up what she wrote, a similar remark in the 1865 article 'Las literatas', and her request to her daughters to burn her manuscripts, which they did; the Women in World History entry confirms the loss of works in progress. The sources frame this as modesty and distrust of her work; whether it reflects high standards cannot be separated from low confidence in her writing, so the score stays near the middle. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 58 / 0.42 to 52 / 0.34 because the behaviour is documented by one biographer and has at least two plausible readings; the cost to her output is real, hence dual-edged.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_rosalia_wiw, src_rosalia_mayoral, src_rosalia_alvarez | 1855-1884 | reference entry, biography, archival journal article] She published poetry in Galician and in Castilian, novels (La hija del mar, Flavio, El caballero de las botas azules, El primer loco), essays and articles (Lieders, Las literatas) (Women in World History); the entry lists lessons in music, drawing and French, Mayoral adds her playing of several instruments and her acting at the Liceo, and Alvarez documents the acting through a surviving volume of twelve staged comedies with her name written in. The range is across literary forms and performance within one cultural field, which keeps the score moderate.

portrait.source: Albumen carte-de-visite photograph of Rosalía de Castro by María Cardarelly, Santiago de Compostela, probably about 1865 (not later than 1866), held in the archive of the Fundación Rosalía de Castro (Padrón), shown on the foundation's 'Imaxes' page and reproduced in its 2013 study by Anxo Angueira, where the print is pasted into a first edition of Cantares gallegos opposite her signed autograph and a pencil note '15-VII-85' (her death date). The file is the Wikimedia Commons upload 'Rosalía Castro de Murguía por María Cardarelly.jpg' (credited to the foundation, 1200 x 1915 pixels), whose pose, earring and hair match the print reproduced in the foundation's study; downscaled to 627 x 1000 with no upscaling. A sibling frontal print in the Real Academia Galega archive carries Cardarelly's studio stamp.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: albumen print made about 1865 by María Cardarelly (born about 1845, died about 1920 according to Wikidata and Wikipedia, so more than 80 years dead under Spain's rule for authors who died before 1987); made and circulated before 1931, so also out of copyright in the United States. The holding foundation states no restriction on this image on its image page, and its legal notice licenses its own content CC BY-SA 3.0 while reserving third-party rights; the Real Academia Galega's record for the sibling print could not be read (see provenance notes).
portrait.attribution: María Cardarelly, portrait of Rosalía de Castro (albumen carte de visite, about 1865), Fundación Rosalía de Castro; downscaled.
portrait.creator: María Cardarelly (photographic studio, Santiago de Compostela)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / SURVIVED IN PART, ROUTE CHANGED: the lead was Commons 'Rosalia de Castro.jpg' (716 x 994, the frontal carte-de-visite, credited to Maria Cardarelly c.1865, source Galiciana record 462909, template PD-old-auto-expired). Cardarelly authorship and c.1865 date are confirmed by two Fundacion Rosalia de Castro studies (Castelao 2017, Angueira 2013): the Real Academia Galega (RAG) print, part of the family fund Gala Murguia deposited at the RAG in 1964, carries the studio stamp 'Fotografia de M.a Cardarelly, Santiago'. HOLDER RECORD: the Galiciana/RAG record (arquivo.galiciana.gal registro.do?id=462909) is behind a script-challenge page (JavaScript cookie challenge, not bypassed; the browser tool refused the host; WebFetch timed out; Hispana returned 429) so no RAG permission or rights statement could be read; this is a BOT WALL, not a rights conflict, and no source read states any restriction on the print. The shipped image is therefore the SIBLING print of the same sitting, held in the archive of the Fundacion Rosalia de Castro (FRC), whose own pages could be read: the 'Imaxes' page lists it, the legal notice (aviso legal) licenses FRC content CC BY-SA 3.0 while reserving third-party rights and states no restriction on this image, and the 2013 FRC study by Angueira reproduces the print pasted into a bound first edition of Cantares gallegos opposite a signed autograph and a pencil note '15-VII-85'. File: Commons 'Rosalia Castro de Murguia por Maria Cardarelly.jpg' (1200 x 1915, credited to the FRC), whose pose, earring and hair match the print reproduced in the FRC study; downscaled to 627 x 1000, no upscaling, not cropped. IDENTITY: no caption on the print; identity rests on the FRC archive attribution, the pencil death-date note and signed autograph in the same book, the stamped RAG sibling, and the Castelao/Angueira studies (both by the foundation that keeps her house and papers); the face matches the RAG frontal print and the two Encausse prints (not downloaded). RIGHTS: albumen print made about 1865 by Maria Cardarelly (born about 1845, died about 1920 per Wikidata/Wikipedia, exact year not confirmed in the FRC study; she would have been about 100 in 1945, so Spain's life+80 rule for authors who died before 1987 has expired in any case); pre-1931 so out of the US term. KIND likeness. DATE c.1865 (Castelao: most plausible 1865, not later than 1866; the Cantares volume of 1863 and an 1864 copied letter bound with the print do not date the photograph). The Commons file for the frontal RAG print and the Brocos painting, Sellier-based drawing and 1880s depictions were not used. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13, Wikidata API) Q464264 label 'Rosalia de Castro', description 'Galician poet and writer (1837-1885)', born 23 February 1837, two death-day values (15 and 22 July 1885; scholarly sources give 15 July), human, citizen of Spain. REGION southern_europe (Spain), ERA 19th_century, nationality ES. KOREAN NAME 로살리아 데 카스트로 is a transliteration choice (no Korean Wikidata label or Korean Wikipedia article; style follows 미겔 데 세르반테스). EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE: nothing about illness, melancholy, psychology, suicidal imagery, or her origins is scored; the Gale entries and Mayoral's biography attribute her moods to her birth and to illness and Mayoral discusses suicide imagery and a 'Polycrates complex' cited from another author; those passages were read and not used. ATTRIBUTION: limited_but_usable (her works and publications are well attributed, but Alvarez Ruiz de Ojeda says no documentary biography exists, Murguia destroyed her letters and shaped her image, and Mayoral warns of a mythified portrait). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Martinez-Rico, Women in World History entry (https://encyclopedia.com/women/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/castro-rosalia-de-1837-1885). READ: both Gale entries (full), Mayoral biography (full), Alvarez Ruiz de Ojeda 2018 (about 60 percent), Castelao and Angueira FRC studies (parts), the FRC image page and legal notice. NOT OPENED: Kulp-Hill's Twayne book, Stevens, Davies, Catherine, the RAG record, Galiciana, Britannica (403), Real Academia de la Historia biography (script page), Spanish and Galician Wikipedia (not used). SOURCE FAMILIES: Gale reference (two entries), Mayoral, Alvarez Ruiz de Ojeda, plus FRC portrait studies; all secondary, no adversarial voice found and no independent contemporary account of her behaviour, so the profile is a sparse 5-row creative profile. CONTRADICTIONS: the two Gale entries differ on whether she was reluctant to publish Cantares gallegos and on her upbringing (aunt or godmother); the date of 'Las literatas' is 1865 (Mayoral) or 1866 (Gale) and is not carded; Mayoral dates her birth 23 February, Gale 24 February. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE (PASS): cards (1) Cantares gallegos, (2) Follas novas and En las orillas del Sar, (3) novels and 'Las literatas'. SELF-CALIBRATION: four rows lowered (two concentration, two self-calibration), no raise flags; see handback.
